finding.claim: Mass assignment on PUT /me: the entire request body is merged into the authenticated user object and saved, so any authenticated user can set privileged fields such as role, isAdmin, id, email, or password hash, enabling privilege escalation or account takeover. The `__proto__` key is also a possible vector. Object.assign with a JSON-parsed own `__proto__` property invokes the setter and changes only the target's prototype, not Object.prototype, so global pollution is unlikely.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled req.body of PUT /me (any authenticated user)
finding.sink: Object.assign(req.user, req.body) followed by req.store.save(req.user), which persists arbitrary fields on the user record

trace.note: Object.assign copies all attacker-supplied body keys onto req.user with no allowlist
The full user object is returned in the response

finding.guards_checked: Only users.js exists in the repo. There is no field allowlist, schema validation, or role/ownership check in this file. Authentication middleware that sets req.user is not in the repo, so it was not verified. The sibling route /me/profile (line 11) destructures only displayName and bio, which shows that an allowlist was intended and is missing here.

verdict.reason: users.js:5 runs Object.assign(req.user, req.body) with no allowlist, and users.js:6 persists it, so any authenticated user can set role or other privileged fields. The sibling route at users.js:11 shows the intended allowlist is missing here. The auth middleware that sets req.user is not in the repo, and no schema validation or role check exists in this file.

verdict_facts.reason: users.js:5 does Object.assign(req.user, req.body) and users.js:6 saves req.user, with no allowlist, schema check or decorator in the file, so any authenticated user can write role/isAdmin-style fields; the allowlist at users.js:11 applies only to /me/profile, and I could not see any control upstream of this directory, so whether role/isAdmin are real fields is unknown.
